title: Romans
intro: 25 days through Paul's letter to the Romans, one passage at a time.

posts.caption: Romans is a letter from Paul to the Christians in Rome, commonly dated around AD 57. Unlike most of his letters, it went to a church he had not founded and had not yet visited. This verse states the theme of the whole letter; "Greek" here stands for all non-Jews. Starting today, 25 days through Romans, one passage at a time.

Paul quotes the prophet Habakkuk here. Martin Luther wrote that grasping what Paul meant by "the righteousness of God" made him feel born again, and the idea became central to the Protestant Reformation. Augustine's conversion in 386 came while reading Romans 13, and John Wesley felt his heart "strangely warmed" in 1738 while hearing Luther's preface to Romans read aloud.

Paul begins his argument that all people, Jews and non-Jews alike, have fallen short of what God asks. He starts with non-Jews: God, he says, can be known through creation itself. Theologians call this "natural" or "general" revelation, the idea that the world points to its maker. Psalm 19 expresses something similar: "The heavens declare the glory of God."

Paul now turns to anyone who condemns others while doing the same things. A few verses later he sums up his point: "God does not show favoritism." Here he describes God's kindness and patience as giving people time; in Paul's framing, that patience is meant to lead to repentance, a change of heart and direction.

The center of Paul's argument so far: Jews and non-Jews stand in the same place, since all have fallen short. "Justified" is a legal term meaning declared in the right, like a verdict of acquittal. "Grace" (charis) means a gift freely given, not earned. And "redemption" was the word for buying back a slave or a captive.

A verse central to the Catholic–Protestant debate. Luther's German Bible read "by faith alone," adding a word not in the Greek, and "faith alone" became a Protestant watchword. Catholic teaching also calls justification God's free gift, but sees saving faith as faith working through love. In 1999, Catholic and Lutheran leaders signed a joint declaration agreeing on basic truths of justification.

Paul turns to Abraham, the ancestor of the Jewish people, quoting Genesis 15:6. His point is that Abraham was counted righteous for trusting God before he was circumcised, so he can be the "father" of believing Jews and non-Jews alike. "Credited" is an accounting word, like a sum entered into someone's account.

Paul has just said that someone might, rarely, be willing to die for a good person. His point is that the love he describes came first, before anyone deserved it. Later in chapter 5, Paul contrasts Adam, whose disobedience brought sin and death into the world, with Christ, whose obedience brings life.

Paul answers an objection: if grace is free, why not keep sinning? His reply uses everyday Roman images of slavery and pay. "Wages" (opsonia) often meant a soldier's pay or rations, earned and owed. The contrast is deliberate: sin pays out what is earned, while eternal life is a gift (charisma), something no one earns.

Paul describes a divided self: knowing what is good and not doing it. Readers have long debated who this "I" is. Augustine first read it as a person living under the law before faith, but later concluded it describes the ongoing struggle of believers, a view Luther and Calvin shared. Many modern scholars see the "I" as a figure of speech for humanity, or Israel, under the law.

Chapter 8 is often called one of the high points of Paul's letters, and it opens by answering the struggle of chapter 7. "Condemnation" is a courtroom word for a guilty verdict and its penalty. The Greek word for spirit, pneuma, appears only a handful of times earlier in Romans, but around twenty times in this chapter alone.

A verse many people turn to in hard times. Ancient manuscripts differ slightly here, and so do translations: some Bibles read "all things work together for good" and others "God works all things together for good." Either way, Paul ties that good to God's purpose, which the next verse describes as being shaped into the likeness of Christ.

The climax of chapter 8. Paul lists everything he can think of, from death and life to angels and "principalities," a word for ruling powers, human or spiritual. Some scholars think "height" and "depth" were terms from ancient astrology for the sky above and below the horizon. His conclusion: nothing in all creation can separate believers from God's love.

In chapters 9 to 11, Paul wrestles with a hard question: why had most of his fellow Jews not accepted Jesus as Messiah, and had God's promises failed? Here he borrows the prophets' image of potter and clay (Jeremiah 18). Reformed (Calvinist) readers often see individual predestination in these chapters; others see Paul describing God's dealings with whole peoples.

posts.display: “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, the word of faith we are proclaiming: that if you confess with your mouth, “Jesus is Lord,” and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved.
posts.caption: Paul borrows Moses' words from Deuteronomy 30:14: the message is near, in the mouth and in the heart. "Jesus is Lord" is thought to be one of the earliest Christian confessions of faith. In the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, "Lord" (kyrios) often stood in for God's own name. A few verses later Paul quotes Joel, the same prophecy Peter quotes at Pentecost in Acts 2.

Paul pictures God's people as a cultivated olive tree rooted in Israel. Non-Jewish believers are like wild shoots grafted in, and he warns them not to look down on the Jewish people. A few verses on he writes that "God's gifts and His call are irrevocable," words the Catholic Church cited in 1965 in Nostra Aetate, the landmark declaration that reshaped Catholic–Jewish relations.

After three chapters on God's plan for Israel and the nations, Paul breaks into praise. The next lines draw on Isaiah and Job, and this short hymn closes the long, closely argued first part of the letter. From the next chapter on, Paul turns to everyday life: how believers treat one another and the world around them.

With "therefore," Paul turns from explaining his message to describing how to live it. His readers knew animal sacrifice from temples, both the Jewish temple in Jerusalem and Rome's many shrines; Paul speaks instead of offering one's whole self. The Greek behind "spiritual service of worship," logike latreia, can also be translated "reasonable service," as in the King James Version.

Two contrasting verbs. "Conformed" means pressed into the shape of a pattern, while "transformed" translates the Greek metamorphoo, the root of the English word metamorphosis. Matthew and Mark use the same verb for Jesus' transfiguration on the mountain. Paul places the change in the mind, in the way a person thinks.

The last line of a chapter full of short sayings about living with others, such as "weep with those who weep." Some echo Jesus' own teaching, like "bless those who persecute you." Just before this, Paul quotes Proverbs on feeding a hungry enemy, which will "heap burning coals on his head," an image whose exact meaning is still debated.

Chapter 13 opens with Paul telling believers to submit to the governing authorities and pay taxes. Written while Nero was emperor, that passage has been read in very different ways through history. Paul then sums up the commandments in one line from Leviticus 19:18: love your neighbor as yourself. This verse is his conclusion, echoing Jesus' own summary of the law.

The believers in Rome were divided over food and holy days: some ate only vegetables, others ate anything; some honored special days, others treated every day alike. Many scholars think the tension was partly between Jewish and non-Jewish believers. Paul asks both sides not to judge each other, and this verse is his reason. The words are used in many Christian funeral services.

As the letter winds down, Paul shares his plans: first Jerusalem, with money collected for poor believers there, then Rome, and on to Spain. Acts tells how he did reach Rome, but as a prisoner. Whether he ever reached Spain is unknown; a letter from Clement of Rome, written around the end of the first century, says Paul reached "the limits of the West," which some take to mean Spain.

The last chapter is a long list of greetings, and it begins with Phoebe, from Cenchrea, a port of Corinth. Many scholars think she carried this letter to Rome. Paul calls her a diakonos, a word that can mean servant, minister, or deacon, and translations differ. He then greets about two dozen people by name, a rare glimpse of ordinary members of the early church.

Andronicus and Junia, fellow Jews who had shared imprisonment with Paul, were believers before he was. Later translators often made Junia a man, "Junias," but early writers such as John Chrysostom praised her as a woman, and most modern translations agree. Whether the pair were outstanding "among" the apostles or well known "to" them is debated. That's Romans. Thank you for reading it with me.
